rationale: B wins because it has cleaner editorial judgment: it kills the tempting lawsuit mashup instead of pretending Deel can own it, and its headline, "Deel's AI will flag whether your contractor is really an employee. It won't say how often it's wrong," goes straight at the publishable tension. A has strong bones, especially "Can a payroll vendor's AI tell you to reclassify a worker — and who's liable when it's wrong?", but it overreaches with "Deel ships a free compliance AI while fighting a corporate-espionage lawsuit" as a pitchable angle. That is a reporter's skeptical context, not necessarily a company-owned story.
gaps_in_A: "Deel ships a free compliance AI while fighting a corporate-espionage lawsuit" is dangerous as an owned angle; the set says not to characterize fault, but still invites a trust story Deel may not be able to pitch without making litigation the headline.
"free compliance AI" overstates the fact pattern. The update says the tool is included for existing customers, not that it is universally free.
"pressures rivals who'd charge for the same capability" is under-supported. The update gives no competitor pricing, so A should have framed that as a question, not a market-pressure claim.
"real-time classification risk engine" is a little dressed up. The update says the tool flags risks as a company hires; it does not establish scoring depth, blocking power, or a real-time workflow.
gaps_in_B: "Deel is now automating that call" overstates the disclosed fact. The update says the tool flags risks; it does not say Deel automates classification decisions.
"It won't say how often it's wrong" is sharp, but slightly prosecutorial. The safer version is that Deel has not disclosed accuracy or audit data, not that the tool literally refuses to say.
"A $12B payroll company just made AI compliance a free feature" maps "included for existing customers" into "free" too broadly. Existing-customer bundling is not the same as general pricing.
"The pricing angle...is the only angle you can pitch this week" is too absolute. A named customer with a real flag could make the customer-story angle pitchable immediately.
